source.title: How Many Features Can a Language Model Store Under the Linear Representation Hypothesis?
source.authors: Nikhil Garg; Jon M. Kleinberg; Kenny Peng

record.tranche_reason: The paper gives theoretical bounds on how many sparse features can be represented and linearly accessed, a different method from empirical neuron-interpretability studies.
record.gate_note: The paper reports theoretical capacity results, not measurements of individual neurons in trained language models. It recalls the classical compressed-sensing result as background, which is not recorded as a study result. Its geometric propositions do not test whether real neurons respond to unrelated inputs.
record.test_reason: This is a purely mathematical paper. It bounds how many k-sparse features d dimensions can linearly represent and linearly decode. It never measures neurons in any trained network and never mentions polysemantic neurons. It never tests whether superposition is why real neurons are polysemantic. Showing that exponential feature packing is possible concerns capacity, which is a related but different construct from V3's causal claim. It is theoretical plausibility for the superposition hypothesis, not a test of any version. The findings are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors prove nearly matching bounds for linear compressed sensing: Ω((k²/log k) log(m/k)) is required and O(k² log m) suffices. They read this as a gap showing linear accessibility is stronger than linear representation. They say the upper bound gives theoretical evidence for the superposition hypothesis. They also show representation and probe directions can differ greatly unless norms are bounded.
record.recipe_differences: The study derives mathematical capacity bounds for sparse linear representations rather than applying an empirical neuron-identification or intervention method.

fits_no_version.finding: Under linear representation and linear accessibility, d = O(k² log m) dimensions suffice for m k-sparse features, while d = Ω((k²/log k) log(m/k)) are required. Exponentially many features fit, but more dimensions are needed than with non-linear decoding (O(k log(m/k))).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Linear representation plus linear accessibility allows exponentially many sparse features per dimension, with dimension roughly quadratic in sparsity k.

fits_no_version.finding: For Boolean sparse features, adding a bias and monotonic activation to the probe does not asymptotically lower the required dimension.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Biased monotonic probes do not asymptotically increase linear-accessible feature capacity for sparse Boolean features.

record.problems: The evidence is theoretical and depends on sparse-feature and linear-representation assumptions; the paper does not test trained networks or measure neuron polysemanticity.
record.rows_left_out: No rows left out. Theorem 1 is cited classical compressed-sensing background rather than a result of this study. Propositions 9 and 11 describe possible feature-vector geometry, not the responses or interpretations of trained neurons.

untested.parts: No vision models or neurons studied.
No language-model MLP neurons, token responses, or layer-wise shares measured.

Whether trained networks actually store more features than neurons, and whether this causes neuron polysemanticity, is not examined. Only the mathematical feasibility of packing features under linear representation and access is shown.
No initialization, regularization, noise, or capacity-sufficient settings studied.
No comparison across activation functions, architectures, or regularization; no performance costs measured.
No activation-range or scoring choices varied.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' with a V3 'supports' label is overturned. The paper supplies a feasibility bound for superposition in an abstract linear model. It does not address neurons, polysemanticity, or the cause of polysemanticity in any trained network. It could be cited as background plausibility for the superposition mechanism but not as evidence on V3. Propositions 9 and 11 on feature geometry are correctly left out.

versions.untested_parts: No image classifiers or vision neurons are studied.
No transformer language models, MLP neurons, token responses, or layer-wise shares are measured.

The results concern mathematical constructions under sparse-feature and linear-representation assumptions, not whether trained networks actually use superposition or whether it causes empirical neuron polysemanticity.
No initialization, regularization, training noise, or capacity-sufficient network is studied.

The paper does not compare neuron polysemanticity shares across architectures, activation functions, or regularization, nor measure performance costs. Its decoder-extension result is recorded under fits_no_version.
No real neurons or their interpretations are examined for a shared feature or related subfeatures.
No activation-range or explanation-scoring choices are varied.

rows.subject: k-sparse linear representation framework (A = B construction)
rows.size_stated: d neurons and m features; d = Oϵ(k² log m)
rows.operation_detail: Derives an upper bound on dimensions sufficient to represent and linearly recover sparse features.
rows.measure: Sufficient embedding dimension for ||AᵀAz − z||∞ < ϵ
rows.note: The authors state this permits an exponential number of features relative to embedding dimension; this is a theoretical bound, not an empirical result on a trained model.
rows.check: Upper bound d = O(k² log m) for a mathematical construction (A = B, random incoherent matrix). It shows superposition is possible, not that neurons in trained networks are polysemantic because of it. It is not a measurement of any system's neurons.

rows.subject: k-sparse linear representation framework (A, B construction)
rows.size_stated: d neurons and m features; d = Ωϵ((k²/log k) log(m/k))
rows.operation_detail: Derives a lower bound on dimensions required for linear recovery.
rows.measure: Necessary embedding dimension for ||BᵀAz − z||∞ < ϵ
rows.note: The paper contrasts this with classical compressed sensing, where non-linear decoding needs a dimension linear rather than quadratic in k. The stated lower-bound result is theoretical.
rows.check: Lower bound on dimensions needed for linear recovery. It is a capacity result about matrices and says nothing about the polysemanticity of trained neurons or its cause.

rows.subject: Boolean k-sparse linear representation framework (A, B construction)
rows.size_stated: d neurons and m features; d = Ω((k²/log k) log(m/k))
rows.operation_detail: Derives a lower bound for linearly separating inputs according to each binary feature.
rows.measure: Necessary embedding dimension for linear separation by feature
rows.note: This is a theoretical extension to binary features, not a measurement on a trained network.
rows.check: Boolean-feature lower bound (Theorem 12). It is a theoretical capacity result with no bearing on observed neuron polysemanticity.

rows.subject: Boolean k-sparse linear representation framework (A, W construction)
rows.size_stated: d neurons and m features; d = Ω((k²/log k) log(m/k))
rows.operation_detail: Shows a lower bound persists when the linear probe has a bias and monotonically increasing activation.

conditions.value: biased linear map followed by monotonic activation

rows.measure: Necessary embedding dimension for feature separation
rows.note: This bears on decoder capacity in the mathematical framework; it does not measure how activation functions change the share of polysemantic neurons.
rows.check: Corollary 13 is a capacity result for biased monotonic decoders. It correctly links to no version. The row itself is accurate; it is a theorem, not a measurement.
